title: Xanthe and the Trail
premise: Kestrel Hartwell flies supply runs into the remote interior, keeping her past sealed behind a cockpit door. When the Alder Creek expedition goes silent, she's the only pilot willing to fly into monsoon weather — and what she finds is her estranged father's abandoned field camp, his journal, and one survivor: a young cartographer named Xanthe who claims to be his protégé. Stranded together as floods close the river and the glacier route won't open for weeks, Kestrel must navigate grief, sabotage within the expedition's backers, and the discovery that her father willed her not money but the map of an unrecorded valley. The story ends at calving season, when Kestrel and Xanthe fly the first survey of that valley out through the ice corridor, choosing each other as family over the inheritance of silence.
about_author: Mirabel Eastwick is the pen name of a former bush-country radio operator who spent six seasons in fly-in communities before turning to fiction. She writes adventure novels about people who measure their lives in weather rather than calendars.

chapters.title: Fuel, Weather, Rumors
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A routine medicine run establishes her world: the airstrip, the gossip economy of small towns, and her careful habit of leaving before anyone gets close. Beat: competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: The Silence on Alder Creek
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The expedition's scheduled check-in doesn't come; the backers pressure her to wait, but she preps the plane against advice. Beat: the pull of obligation she can't name.

chapters.title: Into the Gray
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She threads worsening weather upriver, finds the camp wrecked and empty except for a stranger barricaded in the supply tent. Beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Xanthe
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The survivor explains the flood took the others downstream; she's been rationing and signaling for nine days. Mutual suspicion between pilot and cartographer. Beat: two guarded people sizing each other up.

chapters.title: What the River Took
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. They salvage gear and find her father's waterproof journal among the wreckage. Kestrel hides it. Beat: grief ambushing her mid-task.

chapters.title: Grounded
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The airstrip strip floods; the plane is stuck until waters drop or the glacier route opens. First real argument with Xanthe about whether to stay or walk out. Beat: claustrophobia and friction.

chapters.title: The Leaking Boat
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. They repair an old skiff to reach higher ground; the boat takes on water faster than it should, hinting someone cut it. Beat: unease — this wasn't only weather.

chapters.title: Journal Entries
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, alone at night. She finally reads her father's journal: he was mapping an unrecorded valley and suspected the backers wanted the land, not the science. Beat: the past cracking open.

chapters.title: Monsoon Days
chapters.summary: Both POVs interleaved. Trapped in a trapper's cabin, they trade stories by lamplight; Xanthe reveals she was hired anonymously to verify the map. Beat: found-family warmth kindling.

chapters.title: The Radio Ghost
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A garbled transmission claims the survivors were picked up days ago — meaning whoever is transmitting is lying, or watching. Beat: paranoia arrives.

chapters.title: Upstream Evidence
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. They find fresh boot prints and a discarded satellite phone near the cut boat. Someone from the expedition's backer company is on the river. Beat: fear becomes certainty.

chapters.title: The Valley in the Pages
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The journal's final pages describe the valley — and name Kestrel as the only person her father trusted to finish the survey. Beat: inheritance redefined as responsibility.

chapters.title: Running the Rapids
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Fleeing the watcher, they run the flooded gorge in the patched skiff and nearly lose everything, including the journal. Beat: white-knuckle action, trust forged under pressure.

chapters.title: The Watcher
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. They confront the man sent to retrieve or destroy the map; he reveals the backers' land grab and offers Kestrel a buyout. Beat: temptation versus loyalty.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Kestrel burns the buyout offer; Xanthe admits she was originally paid to steal the map and chose not to. Betrayal confessed, forgiveness withheld. Beat: the relationship's lowest point.

chapters.title: Cold Camp
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Silent days waiting for the glacier window; small gestures thaw them — shared chores, Xanthe teaching Kestrel to read contour lines, Kestrel teaching her the radio. Beat: reconciliation without apology speeches.

chapters.title: The Ice Opens
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The glacier calves early; the air corridor will hold for roughly thirty-six hours. They dig out the plane in a race against refreezing meltwater. Beat: hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: First Flight Over the Valley
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Instead of flying straight out, they divert to photograph and record the valley her father died protecting. Beat: the inheritance claimed.

chapters.title: Interception
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The backers' charter plane shadows them; Kestrel uses terrain and weather skill to lose them in the pass her father named after her mother. Beat: climax — mastery, memory, and defiance fused.

chapters.title: Landing
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. They land at the regional strip as the data uploads to a journalist and the land registry simultaneously; the backers' claim collapses publicly. Beat: exhale after the held breath.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She scatters her father's journal copy at Alder Creek, keeps the original, and offers Xanthe a permanent seat in the right-hand cockpit. Beat: grief integrated, family chosen.

chapters.title: Miles and Years
chapters.summary: Both POVs, closing. One year later: the valley is protected, their survey company is small and stubborn, and Kestrel finally measures life in years, not miles. Beat: quiet, earned resolution.
